title: Sitting With It
logline: Every morning before the village wakes, a forest monk walks to the cemetery at its edge and simply sits there, the way he has for years, doing nothing that looks like very much.

object.note: Object 8 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From measuring stillness to keeping death close: a forest monk who sits at a village cemetery every morning before the village wakes.

thread_out.thread: Death kept close each morning opens onto what continues after it: a fisherman's nets, mended for decades, passing to his son.

requirements: A forest hermitage with an established practice of this kind near a working cemetery
A monk willing to be filmed and, if he chooses, to speak about the practice

lesson.in_simple_terms: The texts describe keeping death in mind on purpose, and wisely, as a practice meant to make a person more awake and less grasping, not gloomier. Done carelessly, the same thought only brings grief, glee, numbness or fear.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: මරණය නුවණින් නිතර සිහි කිරීම අඳුරු පුරුද්දක් නොව මිනිසෙකු වඩාත් අවදි කරවන, ඇලීම අඩු කරවන පුහුණුවක් බවත්, නොනුවණින් සිහි කළොත් එයින් ශෝකය, සතුට, නොසැලකිල්ල හෝ බිය පමණක් ඇතිවන බවත් ග්‍රන්ථ කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma describes recollection of death (maraṇānussati) as wisely calling to mind that death is certain for oneself and for every being, and the Pradeepika advises going to charnel grounds and forests to see the dead while doing so. It warns that recollecting without mindfulness, urgency and understanding brings grief for loved ones, glee at an enemy's death, indifference to strangers and fear for oneself, while wise recollection brings a sense of urgency (saṃvega) and understanding. It lists the fruits as heedfulness, less hoarding and stinginess, and dying without fear or confusion, and says the practice reaches only access concentration, never full absorption.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: Morning after morning the monk walks from the hermitage to the cemetery and sits, while the cemetery's ordinary life goes on and villagers pass on the path. The film does not explain; the repetition, and whatever he chooses to say about why he comes, lets the viewer notice that keeping death close can look like calm rather than dread.

key_terms.en: sense of urgency; sober spiritual shock

lesson.caution: It is not 'you only live once, so enjoy it now', nor a comforting 'death positivity'; the texts aim at a sober urgency and warn that brooding on death unwisely does harm.
lesson.builds_on: The last film trained attention toward stillness; this one turns trained attention on death itself, adding that death remembered wisely steadies rather than frightens.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
